source.title: Interpreting Preference Models w/ Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse-autoencoder analysis to a real GPT-J preference model and reports causal effects of SAE-feature ablations on its reward output; it does not test the original toy-network setup.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative outcomes for several ablations, but many plotted reward values are not present in the supplied text. It also describes manually editing completion text and a combined jailbreak, but does not give enough feature-ablation outcome detail for those examples to record as separate rows. The reported layer-20 SAE training metric is not a result about the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The post uses gated SAEs on a GPT-J preference model as a tool to find reward-relevant features and build reward-hacking prompts. Its results are changes in predicted reward after ablating features chosen by attribution patching. That is the method's own performance on a reward-interpretation task, not a measure of whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, or completely and canonically recovered. Feature splitting and incompleteness come up only as the author's speculation, with no measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author concludes SAE features with large causal effects on reward can be found cheaply and used to craft reward-raising prompts. SAE features did not explain all reward differences, and later-layer SAEs were less interpretable. Feature splitting and inefficient compression are offered as possible explanations, not shown.
record.recipe_differences: Trains gated SAEs on a GPT-J preference model and searches/ablates reward-relevant features; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects differed by feature and example: repeating-text ablation had its largest effect on exact repeats, a small effect on paraphrases, and no effect on baselines; URL ablations did not close the reward gap; some “Thank you” cases changed while the last three datapoints did not.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating AtP-selected SAE features shifts the preference model's reward in the expected direction. These ablations do not explain all reward differences (URL, repeating text, 'You're right').
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features on a preference model have causal effects on reward but give an incomplete account of reward differences.

fits_no_version.finding: The layer-20 SAE had very high FVU despite high cos-sim. The author speculates late reward-model layers may not be sparse linear combinations of features. Several URL features had high cos-sim with each other, suggesting redundant or split features. Neither point is quantified as a test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE fit quality, and possibly the sparse-linear representation, degrades in late layers of a reward model.

record.problems: The study uses only one preference model and the top 2k of 155k dataset datapoints with the largest chosen–rejected reward differences. The author notes that the dataset is limited, later-layer SAEs were less interpretable and had worse training metrics, prompts were under 100 tokens and did not cover multiple dialogue rounds, and some SAE effects did not explain the full reward differences. Many plotted numerical outcomes are absent from the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional feature-ablation outcomes could be extracted for the combined jailbreak or the “Putting it all together” examples because the text does not state their specific outcomes.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of it: no capacity analysis of polysemantic neurons.
Whether features are spread across neurons or recoverable as sparse features is assumed. SAEs are used as a tool, and their recovery is not evaluated.
Completeness, stability and canonicality are not measured. Feature splitting is raised only as a hypothesis.
All of it: no comparison of one-dimensional and multidimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4/V5 labels are dropped because the reward-ablation rows measure the preference model's heuristics, using features selected for reward relevance. This is the study's own method performance (T4). Most values are figure-only and absent from the text. The only SAE-quality metrics (L0, FVU, cos-sim) are reported qualitatively per layer and are not framed as a test of any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test toy networks, feature sparsity relative to dimensions, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transitions.
It does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.

It tests whether SAE features in one preference model have causal effects on reward, not whether features generally spread across neurons, how many neurons represent them, or whether the SAE recovers a complete feature set.
The results bear on completeness and feature splitting, but do not test feature stability across models, training runs, or other settings, nor establish canonicality.
It does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The tested GPT-J preference model and the reported SAE-feature ablations
reader_labels.reason: Ablating identified SAE features changed reward in the described direction in several examples, supporting the limited claim that an SAE can recover causally reward-relevant features in this model (r1, r3, r6, r10, r12-r15).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The tested feature-ablation examples and baselines
reader_labels.reason: Some ablations had small or incomplete effects, and other tested cases showed no effect; the study does not establish broad or complete feature recovery (r2, r4, r5, r7-r9, r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Ablations often failed to explain the full reward difference, and the repeating-text result involved more than one feature; this limits any claim that the recovered features are complete units (r6-r10, r12-r15).
